pocket than in it, and two of those were level within a hundredth of a point. At the top are the two players the
sport thinks of first when it thinks of off-script football: Josh Allen (`{python} f"{oqrow('J.Allen').epa_out:+.2f}"` EPA per dropback outside the pocket,
`{python} f"{oqrow('J.Allen').epa_in:+.2f}"` in it) and Patrick Mahomes
(`{python} f"{oqrow('P.Mahomes').epa_out:+.2f}"` and `{python} f"{oqrow('P.Mahomes').epa_in:+.2f}"`). Notice
what kind of skill that is. Both can run, but the value isn't mainly in the running: it is in throwing
accurately on the move, to receivers who know the scramble drill, while the defense is scrambling too. And
notice who is *not* above the line. Jalen Hurts, one of the most dangerous running quarterbacks of the era, sits
well below it (`{python} f"{oqrow('J.Hurts').epa_out:+.2f}"` outside, `{python} f"{oqrow('J.Hurts').epa_in:+.2f}"`
in). Much of his running comes on designed runs and sneaks, which are not dropbacks and so are not in this chart;
running ability and off-script passing are different skills.

Read the chart with two cautions. First, "out of the pocket" includes designed rollouts and bootlegs
([Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)), which are good plays for everyone, so
a quarterback whose offense calls many of them looks better out there for reasons that have nothing to do with
improvisation. Second, it is four seasons of a few hundred plays per quarterback: the order in the middle of the
pack is mostly noise, and only the ends of the chart are worth arguing about.

### A short history: from Tarkenton to Mahomes

The scramble entered the NFL's vocabulary with Fran Tarkenton, a preacher's son from Athens, Georgia, who quarterbacked
the expansion Minnesota Vikings from their first game in 1961. Behind a thin, new offensive line, he ran around
behind it, often for long stretches, until someone came open. Coaches of his era, his own first head coach Norm Van Brocklin among them, thought scrambling undisciplined (the feud with Van Brocklin ended with Tarkenton demanding a trade in 1967);
Tarkenton's answer, preserved on his Hall of Fame page, was that "I scramble because I'm good at it, because I can
twist and dodge those big pass rushers better than most guys, and we get a lot of touchdowns that way." He retired
in 1978 holding the career records for completions, passing yards and touchdown passes.[^tarkenton]

For decades after that the pocket passer was the ideal: the quarterbacks who won the most, from Joe Montana to
Peyton Manning and Tom Brady, did their damage on schedule, and the offenses built around them, timed to the drop,
treated a scramble as a play that had failed. But the off-script line never died. John Elway passed for 3,000 yards
and ran for 200 in seven straight seasons and built a career on late comebacks; Steve Young retired with 43 rushing
touchdowns, then the second-most by any quarterback.[^offscript-hof] Teams with quarterbacks like them practiced what
to do when the play broke.

What changed in the last decade is scale. College football filled with spread offenses and athletic quarterbacks who
had been improvising since high school, and NFL offenses stopped treating the scramble drill as an emergency
procedure and started repping it weekly and designing around it. The quarterbacks who came out of that world
(Mahomes, Allen, Lamar Jackson, Jalen Hurts) made off-script play part of the plan rather than an emergency.

## Getting rid of it: the throwaway

The last of the quarterback's options when nothing is open is the least glamorous and among the most valuable. A
[**throwaway**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-throwaway) is a pass he deliberately throws where nobody can
catch it, usually out of bounds or well over a covered receiver's head, to avoid a sack or an interception. He
gives up the down but keeps the yards. NFL quarterbacks threw the ball away on
`{python} f"{100 * TA_RATE:.1f}%"` of dropbacks from 2022 to 2025.

Why is that a skill and not a surrender? Look at what the alternatives cost. In the same seasons, the average
throwaway was worth `{python} f"{TA_EPA:+.2f}"` EPA (an incompletion, a lost down), the average sack
`{python} f"{SACK_EPA:+.2f}"` (a lost down *and* six or seven yards), and the average interception
`{python} f"{INT_EPA:+.2f}"`. A quarterback who turns two sacks a game into throwaways gains about
`{python} f"{2 * (TA_EPA - SACK_EPA):.0f}"` points a game for his team, without completing a pass.

There is a catch, and it is a rule. [**Intentional grounding**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-intentional-grounding) is a foul for throwing the ball away to avoid a sack
when the pass isn't in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver; it costs a loss of down and ten yards
(or loss of down at the spot of the pass, if that is worse), and a safety if the quarterback throws it from his own end zone. The
rule changes once the quarterback leaves the
[**tackle box**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-box), the area between where the two offensive tackles
lined up: outside it, any pass that lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage (including out of bounds past it) is
legal, receiver or no receiver.[^grounding] [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd)
covers the full rule; here is what it means for the quarterback.

```{python}
#| label: fig-throwaway
#| fig-cap: "Where a throwaway is legal. Left: inside the tackle box (shaded), a quarterback under pressure must throw in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver; throwing it over Y's head, near him, is a legal throwaway (green), while throwing it to an empty part of the field is intentional grounding (red). Right: once he is outside the tackle box, the ball only has to land at or beyond the line of scrimmage, so throwing it out of bounds past the line is legal (green), but a throw that lands short of the line, near nobody, is still grounding (red). The ball is on the right hash, so the right sideline is close."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
# left: inside the box
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -7.6, 0.4, "Q"), O("Y", "TE", 6.0, 5.0)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", -6.6, -1.6, "E"), D("DT", "DT", -5.8, 1.8, "T"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.4, 6.4, "M")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[0], lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-12.5, 14.0), title=False)
clean(axes[0])
tackle_box(axes[0], fld, p, -12.5)
arrow(fld, p, [(-7.6, 0.4), (2.0, 4.6), (10.0, 6.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
arrow(fld, p, [(-7.6, 0.4), (0.0, -5.0), (6.0, -9.6)], color=RED, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
say(fld, p, 11.6, 4.0, "legal: thrown\nnear Y", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 8.4, -7.6, "grounding:\nnobody there", color=RED, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -11.0, 0.0, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6)
axes[0].set_title("Inside the tackle box", loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
# right: outside the box, ball on the right hash
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.0, 11.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", 9.0, 19.0)]
dfn = [D("RE", "DE", -7.4, 8.0, "E"), D("RCB", "CB", 9.6, 20.4, "C")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[1], lateral=(-4.5, 26.5), window=(-12.5, 14.0), title=False)
clean(axes[1])
tackle_box(axes[1], fld, p, -12.5)
arrow(fld, p, [(-6.0, 11.0), (2.0, 19.0), (5.0, 25.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
arrow(fld, p, [(-6.0, 11.0), (-4.6, 17.0), (-3.4, 22.6)], color=RED, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
say(fld, p, 6.4, 11.4, "legal: out of bounds\npast the line", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -9.4, 15.6, "grounding: lands\nshort of the line", color=RED, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 2.4, 10.2, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, -11.0, 0.0, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6)
xs_, ys_ = XY(fld, p, -4.0, 25.0)
axes[1].text(xs_, ys_, "out of bounds", rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
axes[1].set_title("Outside the tackle box", loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The rule rewards exactly the skills this chapter has been describing. A quarterback who climbs and slides inside the
pocket can always find a covered receiver to throw near; a quarterback who escapes the pocket earns the right to
throw it into the stands. The quarterback who gets in trouble is the one who stays in the box with nobody near
him, panics, and flings it at the turf, or who, outside the box, tries to throw it away on the run and doesn't get
it back to the line.

The most famous grounding call of recent decades shows how expensive the panic is. On the New England Patriots' first
offensive play of Super Bowl XLVI, against the New York Giants in February 2012, Tom Brady dropped back from his
own 6-yard line with Justin Tuck bearing down on him, and threw deep down the middle to nobody. The flag came out;
Brady had thrown it from his own end zone, so the grounding penalty was a safety, and the Giants, who had punted
on their own opening drive, led 2-0. They won by four.[^xlvi]

## The checkdown: risk management, not cowardice {#checkdown}

The last read in most progressions is the [**checkdown**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown): a short,
safe throw, usually to a running back or tight end a few yards past the line, underneath all the coverage. It is
the quarterback giving up on the big play to take a small, nearly certain one. Fans boo it. Coaches mostly
don't, and the data says why.

```{python}
#| label: fig-endings
#| fig-cap: "How dropbacks end, and what each ending is worth: every regular-season dropback from 2022 to 2025, grouped by FTN's charting of where the ball went (best average outcome at the top, worst at the bottom; labels give the share of all dropbacks). A quarterback scramble tops the list partly by selection: quarterbacks run when the coverage has left open grass, and when it hasn't, the play lands in the throwaway, sack or interception rows instead. That is why off-script football can look great here and still cost value on average. Among throws, the first read is worth the most and each step down the progression gives up value; the checkdown is worth about nothing on average, which is a great deal better than the three endings below it. A throwaway costs a down, a sack a down and yards, an interception the ball. Interceptions and throwaways are counted on their own, whichever read they were aimed at, so the read rows are completions and incompletions only. Data: FTN charting and nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy."
E = END.sort_values("epa", ascending=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
ys = np.arange(len(E))
cols = [style.SERIES[0] if v >= 0 else style.SERIES[7] for v in E.epa]
cols = [style.MUTED if n.startswith("Designed") else c for n, c in zip(E.index, cols)]
ax.barh(ys, E.epa, color=cols, height=0.62)
for y, (n, r_) in zip(ys, E.iterrows()):
    x = r_.epa
    lab = f"{x:+.2f}   ({r_.share:.1%} of dropbacks)"
    if x < -2.5:      # long bar: label inside it
        ax.text(x + 0.1, y, lab, va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6.9, color="white", fontweight="bold")
    else:
        ax.text(x + (0.06 if x >= 0 else -0.06), y, lab, va="center", ha="left" if x >= 0 else "right",
                fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, E.index, fontsize=7.4)
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax.set_xlim(-4.7, 2.1)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.2)
ax.set_xlabel("EPA per dropback", fontsize=7.8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-endings from the middle out. A checkdown is worth, on average, `{python} f"{END.loc['Checkdown', 'epa']:+.2f}"`
EPA: essentially nothing. It is caught `{python} f"{100 * CHK_COMP:.0f}%"` of the time, thrown about
`{python} f"{CHK_AY:.1f}"` yards past the line, and gains most of what it gains after the catch
(`{python} f"{CHK_YAC:.1f}"` yards on average). That looks like a wasted play only if you compare it to the first
read. The real comparison is to what happens to a quarterback who *doesn't* check the ball down when the first
reads are covered: he holds it, and the next three bars are waiting. The checkdown is the cheapest way to end a
play that has failed.

That is what *risk management* means at quarterback. Each read in the progression has an expected value and a
risk of disaster, and the checkdown is the read with the least of both. A quarterback who takes it at the right
moment gives up a little upside to cut off the tail of sacks and interceptions, and over a season that tail decides
games.

The right moment depends on the situation, and the third-down numbers show how much (2022–2025, share of plays
that gained the first down, and EPA):

| Third down, and the ball goes… | Converted | EPA per play |
|---|---|---|
| 7+ yards to go: to the first read | `{python} f"{100 * R1_3_LONG:.0f}%"` | – |
| 7+ yards to go: checked down | `{python} f"{100 * CHK3_LONG:.0f}%"` | `{python} f"{CHK3_LONG_EPA:+.2f}"` |
| 7+ yards to go: sacked | 0% | `{python} f"{SACK3_LONG_EPA:+.2f}"` |
| 3 or fewer to go: checked down | `{python} f"{100 * CHK3_SHORT:.0f}%"` | – |

On third-and-long, a checkdown usually means a punt. Even so it beats the sack: when the ball is going to be punted
anyway, the yards the back gains after the catch still flip a little field position, while a sack can push a field
goal out of range. On third-and-short the same throw is a good bet. Good quarterbacks know the down and distance on
every snap and adjust: checkdowns early, when four yards on first down keeps the offense
[on schedule](../10-situational-football/10-01-early-downs-and-field-zones.qmd), patience on third-and-long,
when only a throw past the sticks will do.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Checking it down is what scared quarterbacks do." Every great quarterback checks the ball down, often, and good
offenses design their checkdowns to gain yards: a back who catches it in space with one linebacker to beat. The difference between a good checkdown and a bad one is
*when*: a checkdown after the deeper reads were honestly covered is a good decision; a checkdown on the first beat
of a play, before the deep reads had time to open, is a quarterback who has stopped trusting his protection.
Watch where his eyes were before he threw it.
:::

## Measuring a quarterback: time to throw, aDOT, CPOE and EPA

You can now describe a quarterback's process. The data can describe his *style* and his *results*, and four
numbers do most of the work.

- **[Time to throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-time-to-throw)** (seconds from the snap to the release)
  says how long he holds the ball: quick and decisive, or patient and hunting.
- **[aDOT](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-adot)** (average depth of target) says how far downfield he aims:
  underneath and safe, or deep and aggressive.
- **CPOE** says how accurate he is, after allowing for how hard his throws were.
- **EPA per dropback** says what it all adds up to: the points his dropbacks added, sacks, scrambles and turnovers
  included.

The first two describe style, and neither is good or bad on its own; the last two describe results. All four are
public: the Next Gen Stats passing leaderboard (<https://nextgenstats.nfl.com/stats/passing>) has time to throw,
air yards and its own CPOE for every starter, and rbsdm.com (<https://rbsdm.com/stats/>), built on the same
nflverse data as this chapter, has EPA per dropback and CPOE, so you can profile this Sunday's quarterback before
kickoff. The one that needs explaining is CPOE.

### CPOE: completion percentage, corrected for difficulty

Completion percentage is the oldest quarterback number and one of the most misleading, because it rewards easy
throws. A quarterback who checks the ball down all day completes 75% of his passes; one who throws deep outs and
posts completes 60% and may be the better passer. **[CPOE](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cpoe)**, or
**[completion percentage over expected](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-completion-percentage-over-expected)**,
fixes this by comparing each throw with a model's estimate of how often a throw like it is completed. The nflverse
model behind the numbers here knows each throw's depth, which part of the field it went to, the down and distance,
and whether the quarterback was hit as he threw;[^cp-model] the Next Gen Stats version also knows, from tracking
data, how far the receiver was from the nearest defender.[^ngs-xcomp] A deep out to the sideline might have an
expected completion rate of 45%; a checkdown to the flat, 85%. Complete the deep out and you gain 55 percentage
points over expected; drop the checkdown and you lose 85. Average those differences over a season and you have CPOE.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cpoe
#| fig-cap: "Completion percentage and what was expected, 2025 regular season (quarterbacks with at least 300 dropbacks). Each row is a quarterback: the hollow circle is the completion rate the nflverse model expected from his throws, the filled circle is what he actually completed, and the line between them is his CPOE, the number on the right. Rows are sorted by CPOE. Two quarterbacks with the same completion percentage can be far apart once difficulty is counted: find Brock Purdy and Jared Goff, whose filled circles sit at almost the same spot, about 72%, and whose hollow circles do not. Data: nflverse play-by-play (cp and complete_pass) via nflreadpy."
C = Q.sort_values("cpoe")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 0.17 * len(C) + 0.9))
ys = np.arange(len(C))
for y, (_, r_) in zip(ys, C.iterrows()):
    col = style.SERIES[0] if r_.cpoe >= 0 else style.SERIES[7]
    ax.plot([100 * r_.xcomp, 100 * r_.comp], [y, y], color=col, lw=2.2, alpha=0.7, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.plot([100 * r_.xcomp], [y], "o", ms=5, mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.INK_2, mew=1.0)
    ax.plot([100 * r_.comp], [y], "o", ms=5, color=col, mec="white", mew=0.6)
    ax.text(1.06, y, f"{r_.cpoe:+.1f}", va="center", ha="right", fontsize=6.6, color=col,
            transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), clip_on=False)
ax.set_yticks(ys, [f"{r_.label} ({'LAR' if r_.team == 'LA' else r_.team})" for _, r_ in C.iterrows()], fontsize=6.6)
lo_x = 5 * np.floor(100 * min(C.comp.min(), C.xcomp.min()) / 5) - 1
hi_x = 5 * np.ceil(100 * max(C.comp.max(), C.xcomp.max()) / 5) + 1
ax.set_xlim(lo_x, hi_x)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0f}%"))
ax.set_xlabel("completion % (hollow: expected, filled: actual)", fontsize=7.8)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.2)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.text(1.06, len(C) - 0.1, "CPOE", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, fontweight="bold",
        transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), clip_on=False)
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(C) + 0.4)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In 2025 the spread was enormous: `{python} f"{BEST_CPOE.player_first_name} {BEST_CPOE.player_last_name}"`
completed `{python} f"{BEST_CPOE.cpoe:+.1f}"` percentage points over expectation, and
`{python} f"{WORST_CPOE.player_first_name} {WORST_CPOE.player_last_name}"`
`{python} f"{WORST_CPOE.cpoe:+.1f}"`. Purdy and Goff show why the correction matters: Purdy completed
`{python} f"{100 * qb('Purdy').comp:.1f}%"` of his passes and Goff `{python} f"{100 * qb('Goff').comp:.1f}%"`,
but Purdy's throws were expected to be completed only `{python} f"{100 * qb('Purdy').xcomp:.0f}%"` of the time and
Goff's `{python} f"{100 * qb('Goff').xcomp:.0f}%"`, so Purdy's CPOE was `{python} f"{qb('Purdy').cpoe:+.1f}"` and
Goff's `{python} f"{qb('Goff').cpoe:+.1f}"`. Goff threw shorter (an aDOT of `{python} f"{qb('Goff').adot:.1f}"`
yards to Purdy's `{python} f"{qb('Purdy').adot:.1f}"`).

CPOE is the best single public measure of accuracy, and it is steadier from season to season than completion
percentage, but read it with three cautions. It credits the quarterback for everything that is not in the model: a
receiver who makes a great catch, or a scheme that gets receivers wide open, raises it. It says nothing about
*where* the ball went, only whether it was caught: a quarterback who throws safely and accurately to covered
checkdowns can post a fine CPOE and a poor offense. And check what each version does with throwaways. They count
as incompletions in plain completion percentage, which punishes a smart habit, but the nflverse model leaves most
of them out, because only `{python} f"{100 * TA_CP_SHARE:.0f}%"` of charted throwaways get a completion
probability.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Completion percentage measures accuracy." It measures accuracy *and* the difficulty of the throws a quarterback
chooses, mixed together, and difficulty dominates. A conservative passer and an aggressive one can be equally
accurate and be ten points apart in completion percentage. If you want accuracy, look at CPOE; if you want to know
how aggressive he is, look at aDOT; if you want to know whether it worked, look at EPA.
:::

### Whose sack is it?

Sacks are charged to the quarterback's line in the box score, but a good share of them belong to him. FTN's
charters, who watch every sack on video, marked `{python} f"{100 * QB_FAULT:.0f}%"` of the sacks from 2022 to 2025
as the quarterback's fault: held the ball too long, drifted into the rush, missed the hot throw. A cleaner number
separates the line's share from his: *pressure-to-sack rate*, the share of the dropbacks on which he was
[pressured](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure) that ended in a sack. The line decides how often he is
pressured; what happens next is mostly him. From 2023 to 2025 pressured quarterbacks were sacked
`{python} f"{100 * P2S_ALL:.0f}%"` of the time, but among those with 200 or more pressured dropbacks the rate ran
from `{python} f"{100 * P2S.p2s.iloc[0]:.0f}%"` (`{python} P2S.name.iloc[0].split(".")[-1]`) to
`{python} f"{100 * P2S.p2s.iloc[-1]:.0f}%"` (`{python} P2S.name.iloc[-1].split(".")[-1]`).[^p2s] That spread is
pocket presence, measured. [The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) takes up why pressure is the
steadier number and the sack the noisier one.

### The style map

Put time to throw and aDOT on two axes and color each quarterback by his EPA per dropback, and quarterback styles
separate into families.

```{python}
#| label: fig-style-map
#| fig-cap: "Quarterback style map, 2025 regular season: every quarterback with at least 300 dropbacks. Horizontal: average time to throw (Next Gen Stats, snap to release, sacks excluded). Vertical: aDOT, the average air yards of his throws. Color: EPA per dropback (sacks, scrambles and turnovers included), blue above zero and red below. The dashed lines are the averages of the quarterbacks shown, splitting the map into four styles. Every red dot is in the bottom half, but so are some of the season's best quarterbacks: style alone doesn't decide success. Data: nflverse play-by-play and Next Gen Stats via nflreadpy."
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm, LinearSegmentedColormap

cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("epa", [style.SERIES[7], "#f0efec", style.SERIES[0]])
norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=-0.2, vcenter=0.0, vmax=0.3)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.9))
sc = ax.scatter(Q.avg_time_to_throw, Q.adot, c=Q.epa, cmap=cmap, norm=norm, s=46, edgecolor=style.INK_2, lw=0.5,
                zorder=3)
mx, my = Q.avg_time_to_throw.mean(), Q.adot.mean()
ax.axvline(mx, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(my, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1)
x0, x1 = Q.avg_time_to_throw.min() - 0.08, Q.avg_time_to_throw.max() + 0.1
y0, y1 = Q.adot.min() - 0.5, Q.adot.max() + 0.6
ax.set_xlim(x0, x1)
ax.set_ylim(y0, y1)
corner = dict(fontsize=7.6, color=style.MUTED, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(x0 + 0.02, y1 - 0.12, "quick and deep:\nthe rhythm shooter", va="top", ha="left", **corner)
ax.text(x1 - 0.02, y1 - 0.12, "holds it and hunts deep:\nthe aggressive creator", va="top", ha="right", **corner)
ax.text(x0 + 0.02, y0 + 0.12, "quick and short:\nthe distributor", va="bottom", ha="left", **corner)
ax.text(x1 - 0.02, y0 + 0.12, "holds it, throws short:\nthe patient (or stuck) passer", va="bottom", ha="right",
        **corner)
# labels: greedy placement around each point, avoiding earlier labels and the points
fig.canvas.draw()
ren = fig.canvas.get_renderer()
placed = []
pts_disp = ax.transData.transform(np.column_stack([Q.avg_time_to_throw, Q.adot]))
OFFS = [(5, 3), (5, -9), (-5, 3), (-5, -9), (6, -3), (-6, -3), (0, 6), (0, -12), (9, 8), (-9, 8), (9, -13), (-9, -13)]
for i, (_, r_) in enumerate(Q.sort_values("db", ascending=False).iterrows()):
    for dx, dy in OFFS:
        t = ax.annotate(r_.label, (r_.avg_time_to_throw, r_.adot), xytext=(dx, dy), textcoords="offset points",
                        fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, ha="left" if dx > 0 else ("right" if dx < 0 else "center"),
                        zorder=4)
        bb = t.get_window_extent(ren).expanded(1.04, 1.1)
        hits_pts = any(bb.contains(px, py) for px, py in pts_disp)
        hits_lab = any(bb.overlaps(o) for o in placed)
        inside = ax.get_window_extent(ren).contains(bb.x0, bb.y0) and ax.get_window_extent(ren).contains(bb.x1, bb.y1)
        if not hits_pts and not hits_lab and inside:
            placed.append(bb)
            break
        t.remove()
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, fraction=0.035, pad=0.02)
cb.set_label("EPA per dropback", fontsize=7.6)
cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("average time to throw (seconds)", fontsize=8.4)
ax.set_ylabel("aDOT (average air yards per throw)", fontsize=8.4)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.6)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The four corners of @fig-style-map are four ways to play the position.

- **The distributor** (quick and short) wins with decisions: the ball comes out on rhythm to the first open
  receiver, and the offense lives on [YAC](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yac). He rarely takes sacks, and his
  ceiling depends on how many yards his receivers make after the catch.
- **The rhythm shooter** (quick and deep) is the hardest style to play, because deep routes take time to develop;
  it takes anticipation and a scheme that gets receivers vertical fast.
- **The aggressive creator** (holds it, throws deep) extends plays to give deep routes time, with a pocket he
  manages and an off-script game he trusts. His sack rate is higher and his big-play rate too.
- **The patient or stuck passer** (holds it, throws short) is the corner to worry about: the ball comes out late
  *and* short, which usually means the first reads were not open and the quarterback ended up checking it down
  after a long look. Sometimes that is a scheme or a line problem rather than a quarterback problem, but it is
  rarely a good sign.

In 2025 the league MVP, Matthew Stafford, was a rhythm shooter: top-left corner, an aDOT of
`{python} f"{qb('Stafford').adot:.1f}"` yards at `{python} f"{qb('Stafford').avg_time_to_throw:.2f}"` seconds,
and `{python} f"{qb('Stafford').epa:+.2f}"` EPA per dropback. Drake Maye, the runner-up, threw just as deep but held
the ball longer, top-right, with the league's best CPOE and its best EPA per dropback
(`{python} f"{qb('Maye').epa:+.2f}"`). Brock Purdy sits at the far right, just below the average depth line,
holding the ball longer than almost anyone, and still posted `{python} f"{qb('Purdy').epa:+.2f}"`: the patient
passer, not the stuck one.

In 2025 the top half of the map had no red at all; every quarterback below zero threw short. That fits the
argument of [Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) that value lives downfield. But the bottom half also
holds Purdy, Josh Allen and Jared Goff, three of the year's better seasons. Style tells you how a quarterback plays;
the color tells you whether it worked.

## Why the quarterback dominates value

One last number explains why everything in this chapter matters so much, and why the quarterback is paid like no
one else on the field.

First, he touches the ball on almost every play, and on most of them he decides where it goes: in 2025,
`{python} f"{100 * DB_SHARE:.0f}%"` of NFL offensive plays were dropbacks.

Second, passing plays swing further than running plays. Play by play, the EPA of a 2025 dropback had a standard
deviation of `{python} f"{PLAY_SD_DB:.2f}"` points, against `{python} f"{PLAY_SD_RUN:.2f}"` for a designed run:
dropbacks hold the touchdowns and the interceptions. And the player who decides which way they swing differs
more from team to team. Among 2025 starters with 300 or more dropbacks, *average* EPA per dropback had a standard
deviation of `{python} f"{QB_SD:.3f}"`; among ball carriers with 150 or more carries, average EPA per carry had one
of `{python} f"{RB_SD:.3f}"`. Multiply by a season's workload (`{python} f"{QB_N:.0f}"` dropbacks for the median
qualifying quarterback, `{python} f"{RB_N:.0f}"` carries for the median back) and a quarterback one standard
deviation above average is worth about `{python} f"{QB_PTS:.0f}"` points over a season, against about
`{python} f"{RB_PTS:.0f}"` for a back.[^qb-value]

Points become wins at a steady rate: since 2012, each extra win has taken about `{python} f"{PTS_PER_WIN:.0f}"`
points of season scoring margin.[^pts-win] So that quarterback is worth something like
`{python} f"{QB_PTS / PTS_PER_WIN:.1f}"` wins a year over an *average* starter, and the back about
`{python} f"{RB_PTS / PTS_PER_WIN:.1f}"`. Over a *replacement*, the backup a team could sign off the street, the
quarterback's margin is larger still, because the gap between an average starter and a backup is wider at
quarterback than anywhere else (the Purdy and Mac Jones numbers in the film room are one example).

All of these numbers share credit with the blockers, the receivers and the play-caller, and the split is
unknowable from the box score. But the gap is too big to be an accident. The quarterback is the player with the
most chances to add or lose points, on the plays where the most points are at stake. That is the starting point
of [Building a Roster](../14-the-business-of-scheme/14-01-building-a-roster.qmd), where the salary cap turns this
gap into the most important economic fact in the sport.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Tom Brady and Peyton Manning — the pocket as a craft"}
**Peyton Manning, Denver Broncos, 2013.** Manning set the single-season records for touchdown passes (55) and
passing yards (5,477) in 2013, at 37.[^manning-2013] The number that explains how is a quieter one: he was sacked on
`{python} f"{100 * MAN_SR:.1f}%"` of his dropbacks, `{python} "the lowest rate of any regular starter" if MAN_SR_RANK == 1 else f"the {MAN_SR_RANK}th-lowest rate among regular starters"` that season
(the league rate was `{python} f"{100 * LG13_SR:.1f}%"`).[^manning-sacks] Manning had famously little interest in
running. His pocket skill was making the decision before the rush arrived: an elaborate pre-snap read
([The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)) that told him which side to work, then a
progression run so fast that the ball was usually gone before pressure mattered.

**Tom Brady, 2000-2022.** Watch any Brady dropback and look at his feet, not his arm. When the edge closed he moved
up into the pocket a step or two, rarely more, and kept his eyes downfield; when an interior rusher came he slid a
yard and reset. He did it so economically that it looks like nothing happened, which is the point: a quarterback who
climbs well never seems to be under pressure at all. He also got rid of the ball. Even at 44 and 45 his average
time to throw was among the quickest in the league: `{python} f"{brady[2021][0]:.2f}"` seconds in 2021 (rank
`{python} brady[2021][1]` of `{python} brady[2021][2]` qualifying passers) and `{python} f"{brady[2022][0]:.2f}"` in
2022 (rank `{python} brady[2022][1]` of `{python} brady[2022][2]`).[^brady-ttt]

**What to notice:** neither man was a scrambler, and both were extraordinarily hard to sack. Pocket skill is mostly
decision speed and footwork, not escapability.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chiefs 2018 and Bills 2024 — the off-script pair"}
**Patrick Mahomes's left hand.** Monday night, October 1, 2018, at Denver. The Chiefs trailed 23-20 with 3:14 left
and faced third-and-5. Mahomes, in his first season as a starter, was flushed to his left, and Von Miller was
dragging him down. On the way to the ground he switched the ball to his left hand and flipped it to Tyreek Hill
for six yards and a first down. Kansas City scored the winning touchdown seven plays later. Asked years later for
the most impressive play of Mahomes's career, Andy Reid chose that one: a short throw, made with the wrong hand,
with the game on the line.[^lefty]

**Josh Allen's MVP season.** Allen won the 2024 MVP award with a season that mixed both halves of this
chapter.[^allen-mvp] He is enormous (listed at 6-foot-5 and about 237 pounds), fast, and has one of the strongest
arms in the league, which together make the scramble drill unusually dangerous: he can throw 50 yards on the run,
so the deep defenders cannot come up to chase him, and he can run through a tackle, so the underneath defenders
cannot drop off to cover. His early career was full of off-script plays that went wrong (forced throws across his
body, sacks taken while looking for something big). The MVP version still improvises, but the throwaway and the
checkdown are in his game too.

**What to notice:** the two quarterbacks at the top of @fig-off-script got there in different ways. Mahomes's
off-script value is mostly made of throws like the left-handed flip: short, ugly and converting, from a body going
the wrong way. Allen's is power: a throw nobody else can make on the run, or a run nobody wants to tackle. What they
share is the part that took Allen years: off-script talent becomes off-script value only with the judgment to give
up on a play.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New York Giants 2007 season, Super Bowl XLII — the escape"}
February 3, 2008. The Giants trailed the unbeaten Patriots 14-10 and faced third-and-5 at their own 44 with 1:15
left. Eli Manning took the snap in the shotgun and the pocket collapsed: Jarvis Green and Richard Seymour got their
hands on his jersey and should have had the sack. Manning spun free, backed out of the pile, and threw high down
the middle to David Tyree, who had worked back into the middle of the field when his route was disrupted. Tyree
caught it against his helmet with Rodney Harrison draped over him, at the Patriots' 24. The Giants scored four
plays later, on Plaxico Burress's 13-yard touchdown catch, and won 17-14.[^helmet]

**What to notice:** escape and scramble drill together. Manning was no runner; he simply refused to go down and kept
his eyes downfield while he got loose. Tyree did what the drill tells a receiver to do when the play breaks: get to
open grass in the quarterback's line of sight, on a different level from everyone else.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Cincinnati Bengals 2024 — Joe Burrow's timing"}
Joe Burrow led the NFL in passing yards (`{python} f"{BURROW_YDS:,.0f}"`) and touchdown passes
(`{python} f"{BURROW_TD:.0f}"`) in 2024.[^burrow-2024] Burrow can extend plays (he is one of the few quarterbacks
above the diagonal in @fig-off-script), but that season was built in the pocket, on the gifts of the first half
of this chapter: anticipation (throwing outs and digs before the receiver breaks, especially to Ja'Marr Chase, whose timing he has
known since they were college teammates at LSU) and subtle movement in the pocket (a step up, a half-slide) that buys
the extra beat for the throw.

**What to notice:** on replays of Bengals completions, freeze the frame at the release and find the receiver. Very
often he hasn't turned around yet.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers 2023 — Brock Purdy and the system-quarterback debate"}
Brock Purdy was the last player chosen in the 2022 draft, number 262, the pick nicknamed "Mr. Irrelevant."[^purdy]
In 2023, his first full season as the starter, he led the `{python} N23` quarterbacks with 250 or more dropbacks in EPA per
dropback (`{python} f"{PURDY.epa:+.2f}"`, rank `{python} PURDY_EPA_RK`) and in the nflverse model's CPOE (rank
`{python} PURDY_CPOE_RK`). The argument about him since has been whether those numbers are his or Kyle Shanahan's:
a scheme famous for motion, play-action and receivers who run after the catch, with Christian McCaffrey, Deebo
Samuel, Brandon Aiyuk and George Kittle to throw to. Is he a "system quarterback"?

The data cuts both ways, which is why the argument never ends. Against the "YAC merchant" version of the charge: in
2023, `{python} f"{100 * PURDY.yac:.0f}%"` of his receiving yards came after the catch, about the league rate
(`{python} f"{100 * LG23_YAC:.0f}%"`), and his aDOT (`{python} f"{PURDY.adot:.1f}"`) was above the league average
(`{python} f"{LG23_ADOT:.1f}"`). He was throwing downfield and completing it. For the charge: the two CPOE models
disagreed. The nflverse model, which doesn't know how open the receiver was, ranked him first; Next Gen Stats'
model, which does, ranked him `{python} PURDY_NGS_RK`th. That is still very good, but the gap between the two
rankings is the point: part of what the first model credited to Purdy's accuracy was receivers being open, which
the scheme creates. And in 2025, when a turf-toe injury cost Purdy eight games,[^purdy-toe] his backup Mac Jones ran
the same offense at `{python} f"{SF_JONES['mean']:+.2f}"` EPA per dropback, against Purdy's
`{python} f"{SF_PURDY['mean']:+.2f}"`: worse, but far better than Jones's `{python} f"{MJ_PRIOR:+.2f}"` across
2022–2024 with New England and Jacksonville.

**What to notice:** the question "is it the quarterback or the system?" is the right one to ask, and CPOE models that
know about separation help answer it. But a quarterback who throws on time to the right read is part of what makes
a system work. Watch Purdy's anticipation on intermediate throws and judge for yourself.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Watch the eyes.** On replays, especially the end-zone camera that looks straight at the quarterback, count
how many reads he got through before he threw.

- **Find his first look.** Where do his eyes (and his helmet's facemask) point as his drop ends? That is usually
  read 1. Did the ball go there? More than half the time it does.
- **Count the head turns and hitch steps.** Each snap of the head to a new area, usually with a hitch step, is a
  new read. One look and a throw: a rhythm throw. Two or three: a progression. A long stare at one side: he was
  waiting for something to open, he was confused, or he was holding a defender with his eyes on purpose, a
  [look-off](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-look-off) ([Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)).
  His eyes can lie; the ball can't.
- **Note the time.** Count "one-Mississippi" from the snap. Ball out by about two and a half: quick game or first
  read. Out after three: off schedule, or a deep shot with
  [max protection](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-max-protect).
- **Watch his feet when the edge closes.** Step up (climb)? Slide? Or drift back into the rush? The good ones move
  forward.
- **When he leaves the pocket, watch the receivers.** Did the deep ones come back and the short ones go deep? Is
  everyone moving toward his side? That is the scramble drill. Who got open?
- **Judge the ending.** A checkdown on third-and-12 is a punt with a few extra yards; on first-and-10 it is a fine
  play. A throwaway when nothing is there is a small win. A sack after a long hold in a clean pocket is on the quarterback;
a sack that arrives before he could have thrown is on the protection.

**For your prediction log:** for one quarter, write down for each dropback how many reads the quarterback got
through (1, 2, 3, or "off script"), and whether the ball came out on time. By the end you will know which kind of
quarterback you are watching.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the pocket at two seconds"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-pocket
#| fig-cap: "Freeze frame, about two seconds after the snap. Both ends have run their arcs and the tackles have pushed them deep. On the right, the defensive tackle has driven the right guard back about two yards. The left side of the interior is holding. The quarterback (ringed) is at his launch point, eight yards deep."
S = {"LT": (-7.0, -4.9), "LG": (-2.0, -1.8), "C": (-1.9, 0.0), "RG": (-3.9, 1.6), "RT": (-7.0, 4.9),
     "QB": (-8.0, 0.0), "LE": (-9.0, -6.2), "NT": (-0.4, -0.9), "DT": (-2.3, 2.1), "RE": (-9.0, 6.2)}
off = [O(k, k, *S[k], "C" if k == "C" else ("Q" if k == "QB" else "")) for k in OL_KEYS + ["QB"]]
dfn = [D(k, "DE" if k in ("LE", "RE") else "DT", *S[k], "E" if k in ("LE", "RE") else "T")
       for k in ("LE", "NT", "DT", "RE")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=10)
p.highlight("QB")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-12.2, 3.6), title=False, width_in=5.8)
clean(fld.ax)
for sg in (-1, 1):
    arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, 5.4 * sg), (-3.0, 7.2 * sg), (-7.0, 7.4 * sg), (-9.0, 6.2 * sg)], color=style.DEFENSE,
          lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, 2.35), (-1.5, 2.15)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
plt.show()
```

**Where should the quarterback go: back, up, left, right, or out of the pocket?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Up, and a little to his left: climb into the space behind the left guard and the center.** Read the rush picture
piece by piece. The ends have been pushed past him, so drifting back walks him into them, and escaping outside means
running around a rusher who is already at his depth. The right side of the interior is caving: the tackle has the
right guard two yards deep, so stepping straight up, or up and right, takes him into that collision. The left side of
the interior is holding firm, and that is where the cup still has room.

So he climbs at an angle, a step or two up and half a step left, which is a climb and a slide at once. He doesn't have
to leave the pocket, his eyes stay downfield, and he is still inside the tackle box, so if nothing is open he can
still throw it near a covered receiver or check it down. Escaping would only be right if the left side collapsed too.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: third-and-9 at the 31"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-grounding
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-9 at the opponent's 31-yard line, so a field goal would be about a 48-yard try. The quarterback has escaped to his right, outside the tackle box (shaded), with the right end chasing him. Z, his only receiver on that side, is running down the sideline with the cornerback on top of him; Y is covered underneath by the Mike. There is no running room to the first-down line: the Will has come up to spy him (to mirror the quarterback and tackle him if he runs)."
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.5, 10.5, "Q"), O("Y", "TE", 5.0, 8.0), O("Z", "WR", 12.0, 19.5)]
dfn = [D("RE", "DE", -8.0, 7.2, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.6, 9.2, "M"), D("RCB", "CB", 13.4, 19.0, "C"),
       D("WILL", "WILL", 1.8, 12.6, "W"), D("FS", "FS", 17.5, 9.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=79, ball_y="right", to_go=9)
p.highlight("QB")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-10, 27), window=(-12.0, 21.0), title=False, width_in=5.8)
clean(fld.ax)
tackle_box(fld.ax, fld, p, -12.0)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 0.0), (-7.6, 5.0), (-6.5, 10.5)], color=GREEN, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=9)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.4, 4.0), (-8.0, 7.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, head=7, alpha=0.8)
say(fld, p, -10.6, 0.0, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, 9.0, 2.0, "line to gain", color=style.INK_2, fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, 1.7, -3.4, "ball at the opponent's 31", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, 4.0, 25.4, "out of\nbounds", color=style.INK_2, fs=6.2, box=False)
plt.show()
```

**What should the quarterback do with the ball, and is it legal?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Throw it away, out of bounds past the line of scrimmage, and kick the field goal. It is legal because he is outside
the tackle box.** Walk through his options. Z is covered with the cornerback on top, so a throw to him is a
[contested catch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-contested-catch) at best and an interception at worst, and an interception here throws away a likely three points. Y is covered
by the Mike underneath. Running gets nowhere near the line to gain with the Will spying him (shadowing him, ready to tackle). The sack is the
disaster that's easiest to miss: an eight-yard sack pushes a 48-yard field goal back to about 56 yards, where even
good kickers miss often.

So the ball goes out of bounds beyond the line of scrimmage, ideally over Z's head toward the sideline. From inside
the tackle box that throw would have to land near an eligible receiver; from where he is, outside the box, it only
has to reach the line. A throwaway costs a down, which on third down he was about to lose anyway, and keeps every
yard. That is exactly the bargain in @fig-endings: a throwaway at about `{python} f"{TA_EPA:+.1f}"` EPA against a sack at
about `{python} f"{SACK_EPA:+.1f}"`.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: he breaks left"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-scramble
#| fig-cap: "The called play has broken down and the quarterback (ringed) has escaped to his LEFT. The receivers are shown where they are at that moment, with their called routes as grey dashes: X (left outside) was running a go and is 19 yards deep; H (left slot) was on a 5-yard hitch route; Y was running a 12-yard dig from the right that has reached the middle; Z (right outside) was running a 12-yard curl on the far side. The quarterback is right-handed. The defense is not shown."
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.8, -8.6, "Q"), O("X", "WR", 19.0, -15.5), O("H", "WR", 5.0, -8.0),
                O("Y", "TE", 12.0, 2.0), O("Z", "WR", 12.0, 14.5)]
p = Play(off, [], los=LOS, to_go=None)
p.highlight("QB")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 19), window=(-11.0, 24.5), title=False, width_in=5.8)
clean(fld.ax)
called = {"X": [(-0.7, -15.0), (19.0, -15.5)], "H": [(-1.5, -8.5), (5.6, -8.5), (5.0, -8.0)],
          "Y": [(-1.5, 8.5), (12.0, 8.5), (12.0, 2.0)], "Z": [(-0.7, 15.0), (13.0, 15.0), (12.0, 14.5)]}
for k, pts in called.items():
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=2)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 0.0), (-7.8, -4.0), (-6.8, -8.6)], color=GREEN, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=9)
say(fld, p, -9.3, -3.0, "he breaks left", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

**Using the scramble-drill rules, where should each of X, H, Y and Z go, and where will the quarterback look
first?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**X comes back down the left sideline; H takes off deep; Y keeps crossing to the left at his depth; Z works back
across the field, deep. The quarterback looks first at the throws he can make on the move, X coming back and Y
crossing toward him, and takes the deep shot to H or Z only if he can set his feet.**

Settle each receiver by side first, then depth.

- **X** is on the scramble side and deep, so he comes back: he stops his go route and works back toward the line
  of scrimmage along the left sideline, settling at about 8 to 10 yards, into the space his cornerback (running
  deep with him) leaves behind.
- **H** is on the scramble side and short, so he goes deep: he turns up the field from his hitch route, behind the
  defenders who have turned to chase the quarterback.
- **Y** is a crosser, already moving toward the scramble side, so he keeps crossing toward the quarterback, at
  about 12 yards: a level between X coming back and H going deep.
- **Z** is on the backside. Standing on a curl 30 yards from the quarterback is useless, so he runs back across the
  field, deep, into the middle the defense has emptied, and into the quarterback's line of sight.

That gives four receivers at four depths: H deep, Z deep and crossing, Y at about 12, X at 8 to 10, all moving
toward the quarterback's side. Now the look order. He is right-handed and rolling left, so before he can throw at
all he has to turn his hips and square his shoulders back toward the target. The short, firm throws toward the
sideline he is running at, X coming back and Y crossing, are the ones he can make like that. H and Z are the big
play, worth it only if the rush gives him time to stop and set. If all four are covered he has two good options
left: run, if there is grass to the line to gain, or throw it out of bounds past the line; he is outside the
tackle box. What he must not do is throw back across his body to the right.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **The quarterback's eyes run on his feet's clock.** Protection check at the snap, read 1 on the last step of the
  drop, a hitch step for each later read, then the checkdown. Each later read costs about half a second, and value.
- **Each read is answered by a defender, and the ball leaves before the receiver is open.** The quarterback looks
  at the key defender for each read. An anticipation throw, released before the break, beats the defenders'
  reaction; a "see it, throw it" ball arrives a hitch step late into a closing window.
- **Pocket movement is a response to the rush picture.** Edges pushed past: climb. Pressure from one side: slide.
  Interior collapsed: escape, usually outside the tackle on the side the end was run past. Eyes stay downfield
  throughout.
- **Off-script football is coached.** The scramble drill (short goes deep, deep comes back, go where he goes,
  backside comes across deep, the back leaks out) turns a broken play into a second play. Off script is high
  variance: for most quarterbacks it nets out below the pocket; for a few (Allen, Mahomes) it adds value.
- **Bad endings have a price list.** A checkdown is worth about nothing, a throwaway a down, a sack a down and yards,
  an interception the ball. Throwaways must avoid intentional grounding: near a receiver inside the tackle box, past
  the line of scrimmage outside it.
- **Four numbers profile a passer.** Time to throw and aDOT describe style; CPOE (completions over expected) and EPA
  per dropback describe results. Because he decides most plays, and passing varies more than running, the
  quarterback swings more points than anyone else on the field.

- Ron Jaworski with Greg Cosell and David Plaut, *The Games That Changed the Game* (2010): seven landmark game plans broken down from
  the coaches' film, by a former NFL quarterback and two NFL Films producers who spent careers studying all-22 tape.
- Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015) and the Smart Football archive: short essays on progressions,
  reads and how quarterbacks are taught to see the field.
- The all-22 "coaches film" on NFL+ Premium, which shows every player on every snap from above: the only way to
  check a quarterback's progression against what was actually open.
- Ben Baldwin's open-source work on the nflverse CPOE and EPA models (Open Source Football), and the Next Gen Stats
  passing leaderboards for time to throw, aggressiveness and completion probability.
:::

[^ftn-oop]: FTN charting via nflverse (`is_qb_out_of_pocket`), merged with nflverse
    play-by-play; regular-season dropbacks 2022–2025, spikes removed. (A spike is the quarterback throwing the ball
    straight into the ground just after the snap to stop a running clock; the grounding rule allows it, so it is not a
    real dropback. See [The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd);
    Daniel Tomaro, "What Is Intentional Grounding in the NFL?," Pro Football Network, February 8, 2026:
    <https://www.profootballnetwork.com/nfl-intentional-grounding-penalty-details/>.) "Out of the pocket" includes
    designed rollouts as well as escapes. The pressure comparison uses participation data's `was_pressure` flag,
    2023–2025 only, when FTN supplies it; every sack in those seasons is flagged as pressured. Author's calculation
    via nflreadpy. FTN data dictionary: <https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html>;
    participation: <https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_participation.html>.

[^scramble-rules]: The rules here are the common core described in coaching and scouting glossaries, for example
    Inside the Pylon / Scouting Academy, "ITP Glossary: Scramble Drill" (<https://scoutingacademy.com/itp-glossary-scramble-drill/>),
    and Win With The Pass, "The Scramble Drill" (<https://winwiththepass.com/?p=3138>): "If you are shallow go deep, If
    you are deep come back," get into the quarterback's field of vision. Each team's version differs in its details.

[^ngs-sep]: Author's calculation from Next Gen Stats receiving data via nflverse (`load_nextgen_stats`, regular
    seasons 2018–2025, receivers and tight ends with at least 50 targets): a least-squares fit of catch percentage on
    average separation and average intended air yards. NGS defines separation as "the distance (in yards) measured
    between a WR/TE and the nearest defender at the time of catch or incompletion":
    <https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_nextgen_stats.html>. This is a season-average relationship
    across receivers, not a play-by-play estimate.

[^ineligible]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 8, Section 3, Article 1 ("Ineligible Player Downfield": on
    a play with a legal forward pass, a foul if the entire body of an ineligible offensive player is more than one
    yard beyond the line of scrimmage before the pass is thrown, unless he is still blocking a defender he engaged
    at the line; five yards from the previous spot): <https://operations.nfl.com/rules-officiating/2026-nfl-rulebook>.
    [RPOs](04-06-rpos.qmd) covers the rule and its exception.

[^forward-pass]: NFL Rule 8, Section 1: a legal forward pass must be thrown from in or behind the neutral zone; a
    forward pass thrown from beyond the line is illegal (five yards from the spot of the pass and loss of down).
    NFL rulebook: <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^offscript-hof]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "John Elway" ("the only player in National Football League history to
    pass for more than 3,000 yards and rush for more than 200 yards in the same season seven consecutive times";
    "Elway's record 47 fourth quarter game-winning or game-tying drives"):
    <https://www.profootballhof.com/players/john-elway/>; and "Steve Young" ("4,239 rushing yards and 43 rushing
    touchdowns, both the second-most by a quarterback in pro football history at the time of his retirement"):
    <https://www.profootballhof.com/players/steve-young/>.

[^p2s]: Author's calculation via nflreadpy. QB-fault sacks: FTN charting `is_qb_fault_sack`, regular seasons
    2022–2025. Pressure-to-sack rate: sacks divided by dropbacks with participation `was_pressure` true, regular
    seasons 2023–2025, quarterbacks with at least 200 pressured dropbacks; spikes removed.

[^pts-win]: Author's calculation from nflverse schedules (`load_schedules`), regular seasons 2012–2025: a
    least-squares fit of team wins (ties as half) on season point differential across all team-seasons.

[^tarkenton]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "Fran Tarkenton" (career 1961–1978 with the Vikings and Giants; four
    touchdown passes and a touchdown run off the bench in the Vikings' first game, a 37–13 win over Chicago; records
    at retirement; the quoted line on scrambling; his style "often frustrated Vikings coach Norm Van Brocklin, who
    favored a more traditional approach"): <https://www.profootballhof.com/players/fran-tarkenton/>. His father, Dallas
    Tarkenton, was a Pentecostal minister, and he grew up in Athens, Georgia; the Van Brocklin feud ended with
    Tarkenton's trade demand and Van Brocklin's resignation in February 1967: "Fran Tarkenton," Wikipedia,
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Tarkenton>.

[^grounding]: NFL Rulebook, Rule 8, Section 2 (intentional grounding): a foul if a passer facing an imminent loss of
    yardage throws a pass not in the direction and vicinity of an originally eligible receiver; not called when a
    passer who is or has been outside the pocket area throws a pass that lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage
    extended, including out of bounds. Since the 2024 rulebook a passer counts as outside the pocket area if any part
    of his body or the ball is outside it (Rule 3, Section 25 defines the pocket area as between the outside edges of
    the normal tackle positions). Penalty: loss of down and 10 yards from the previous spot, or loss of down at the
    spot of the pass if that is worse; a safety if the passer's entire body and the ball are in his own end zone.
    2026 Official Playing Rules, Rule 8, Section 2, Article 1 (Item 1 and Penalty):
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>. On the 2024 wording change: Mike Florio, "New rule book
    subtly makes it easier for quarterbacks to throw ball away," ProFootballTalk, July 31, 2024:
    <https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/new-rule-book-subtly-makes-it-easier-for-quarterbacks-to-throw-ball-away>.

[^xlvi]: "Super Bowl XLVI," Wikipedia (the Giants' opening drive ended in a punt that pinned the Patriots at their own 6; Brady flagged for intentional
    grounding in the end zone under pressure from Justin Tuck, a safety; Giants won 21–17):
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XLVI>.

[^cp-model]: Ben Baldwin, "nflfastR EP, WP, and CP models," Open Source Football (Sept 2020), describing the
    completion-probability model behind the `cp` and `cpoe` columns:
    <https://www.opensourcefootball.com/posts/2020-09-28-nflfastr-ep-wp-and-cp-models/>.
    The model's features: air yards (and whether they are zero), distance to the sticks, yard line, down, yards to go,
    pass location (middle or not), whether the quarterback was hit, home team, roof type and era.

[^ngs-xcomp]: NFL.com, "Next Gen Stats: Introduction to Completion Probability" (more than ten tracking-based factors,
    including the distance between the receiver and the nearest defender, the distance to the nearest pass rusher and
    the air distance of the pass):
    <https://www.nfl.com/news/next-gen-stats-introduction-to-completion-probability-0ap3000000964655>.

[^qb-value]: Author's calculation, nflverse play-by-play, 2025 regular season: EPA per dropback (sacks and scrambles
    included) for passers with at least 300 dropbacks; EPA per carry on non-dropback runs for ball carriers with at
    least 150 carries. A rough comparison of spreads, not a measure of individual credit; see
    [Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd).

[^manning-2013]: "2013 Denver Broncos season," Wikipedia (Manning's 55 touchdown passes and 5,477 passing yards, both
    single-season records): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Denver_Broncos_season>. Both still stood after the
    2025 season (author's check of nflverse player stats: the closest since are Mahomes's 50 touchdowns in 2018 and
    Brady's 5,316 yards in 2021; Brees's 5,476 in 2011 fell one yard short).

[^manning-sacks]: Author's calculation, nflverse play-by-play, 2013 regular season: sacks per dropback, passers with at
    least 300 dropbacks.

[^brady-ttt]: Next Gen Stats average time to throw (snap to release, sacks excluded), regular season, passers with at
    least 300 attempts, via nflverse/nflreadpy (`load_nextgen_stats`).

[^lefty]: CBS Sports, "Patrick Mahomes' greatest play was this short throw, according to Chiefs coach Andy Reid"
    (third-and-5, 3:14 left, trailing 23–20; six-yard completion to Tyreek Hill while being dragged down by Von
    Miller; winning touchdown seven plays later): <https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/patrick-mahomes-greatest-play-was-this-short-throw-according-to-chiefs-coach-andy-reid>.
    Final score 27–23: ESPN, <https://africa.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/24866002/patrick-mahomes-sparks-chiefs-comeback-win-broncos>.

[^helmet]: "Helmet Catch," Wikipedia (third-and-5 at the Giants' 44 with 1:15 left; Seymour and Green nearly sacked
    Manning; Tyree thrown off his route and drifting to the middle; a 32-yard completion; Tyree pinned the ball to his
    helmet with Rodney Harrison defending; Patriots leading 14–10): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmet_Catch>.
    That article puts the ball at the Patriots' 25, but a 32-yard gain from the Giants' 44 ends at the 24, which is
    where "David Tyree," Wikipedia, puts it ("moved the Giants to the Patriots' 24-yard line with 59 seconds left
    ... Four plays and 24 seconds later, Manning threw a 13-yard touchdown pass to Plaxico Burress"):
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Tyree>.

[^allen-mvp]: NFL.com, "Bills QB Josh Allen wins 2024 AP NFL Most Valuable Player award":
    <https://www.nfl.com/news/bills-qb-josh-allen-wins-2024-ap-nfl-most-valuable-player-award>.
    Height and weight (6-foot-5, 237 pounds) as listed on the 2025 roster in nflverse (`load_rosters`).

[^burrow-2024]: Passing yards and touchdown passes from nflverse play-by-play, 2024 regular season (author's
    calculation via nflreadpy; Burrow ranked first in both, with 4,918 yards and 43 touchdowns). Burrow and Chase
    were teammates at LSU in 2018 and 2019.

[^purdy]: NFL.com, "Mr. Irrelevant: 49ers select Iowa St. QB Brock Purdy to end 2022 NFL Draft":
    <https://www.nfl.com/news/mr-irrelevant-49ers-select-iowa-st-qb-brock-purdy-to-end-2022-nfl-draft>. The 2023 and
    2025 numbers are the author's calculations from nflverse play-by-play and Next Gen Stats.

[^purdy-toe]: Purdy played in 9 of the 49ers' 17 games in 2025 (nflverse player stats). On the turf-toe injury,
    suffered in Week 1 and aggravated in his Week 4 return: NBC Bay Area, "John Lynch states Brock Purdy, 49ers
    'encouraged' by QB's toe injury progress," October 23, 2025:
    <https://www.nbcbayarea.com/news/sports/nfl/san-francisco-49ers/brock-purdy-john-lynch-2/3969197/>.
